title: Al-Khwarizmi and the Birth of Algebra
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Few words in the modern world are used as often as algorithm and algebra, and both come from a single man who lived more than twelve hundred years ago. Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi was a mathematician, astronomer and geographer, and he is often called the father of algebra. He was born around the year 780, probably in Khwarazm, a region which today lies partly in Uzbekistan, and the name al-Khwarizmi simply means from Khwarazm. Little is known about his private life, but his work was so influential that it shaped the way in which people in many countries have calculated ever since.

Al-Khwarizmi spent most of his career in Baghdad, then the largest city in the world and the capital of the Islamic empire. The ruler, Caliph al-Ma'mun, had founded a great centre of learning, known as the House of Wisdom, where scholars gathered from many countries to translate Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic and to carry out new research. Al-Khwarizmi worked there as a scholar, supported by the Caliph, and he studied mathematics, astronomy and geography. The House of Wisdom produced a flood of discoveries, and historians sometimes call this period the Golden Age of Islamic science.

His most famous book was written around the year 820, with the title The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing. Its purpose was practical: the Caliph wanted a guide to the problems that ordinary people faced, such as dividing an inheritance, measuring land and calculating the amount of a tax. Al-Khwarizmi showed how such problems could be turned into equations and solved by clear, step-by-step rules. He described six types of equation, and for each he explained a method of solution, using diagrams to show why the method worked. The book contained no symbols; the equations were written in words, and the reader had to follow the argument in sentences.

The word algebra comes from the title of the book. In Arabic, the process of completion, which means moving a quantity from one side of an equation to the other, was called al-jabr. When the book was translated into Latin in the twelfth century, the word became algebra, and it has been used in this sense in European languages ever since. The second part of the title, balancing, refers to the idea that an equation must remain balanced like a pair of scales: whatever is done to one side must be done to the other. This simple principle, which students learn at school today, is the foundation of all algebra.

Al-Khwarizmi also wrote a book explaining the number system that had been invented in India, with the nine digits and zero. Before it, many people used Roman numerals or counting boards, which made large calculations slow and difficult. The Latin translation of the book, which began with the words Dixit Algorismi, meaning Al-Khwarizmi said, spread the new numbers across Europe. His name, in its Latin form Algorismi, became the word algorithm, which today means any set of step-by-step rules for solving a problem, from a recipe to the programs in a computer.

His interests were wide. He compiled astronomical tables, which gave the positions of the sun, moon and planets, and they were used by astronomers for centuries. He also wrote a work on geography, listing the coordinates of hundreds of cities and rivers, and he helped to prepare a map of the known world for the Caliph. Some historians believe that he took part in an expedition to measure the size of the Earth. Dr Farida Yusupova, a historian of mathematics, says that his greatest gift was clarity: he took ideas that were scattered and complicated and presented them in a form that anybody could use.

Today al-Khwarizmi is remembered in many ways. A statue of him stands in the old city of Khiva, near the place where he is thought to have been born, and a university in Urgench carries his name. Dr Yusupova points out that every time someone solves an equation, searches the internet or follows a recipe, he or she is using an idea that goes back to the scholar of Khwarazm. She hopes that young people in Central Asia will take pride in this heritage, and she adds that the best way to honour him is not to admire his statue but to study the subject that he loved.
